spūmo , āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and
I.a. [spuma].
I. Neutr., to foam, froth (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): caeruleum spumat sale, Enn. ap. Gell. 2, 26 (Ann. v. 378 Vahl.): “maria salsa spumant sanguine,” id. Non. 183, 19 (Trag. v. 145 ib.): “fluctu spumabant caerula cano,” Verg. A. 8, 672 : “adductis spumant freta versa lacertis,” id. ib. 5, 141 ; cf. Lucr. 3, 493: “spumans aper,” Verg. A. 4, 158 ; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 2, 243: Amasenus spumabat,
Verg. A. 11, 548: “equus spumat habenis,” Luc. 6, 399 : “pocula bina novo spumantia lacte,” Verg. E. 5, 67 : “patera,” id. A. 1, 739 ; cf.: “spumat plenis vindemia labris,” id. G. 2, 6 : “spumans bilis,” Cels. 7, 23 ; Plin. 32, 7, 25, § 78: “terra respersa aceto spumat,” foams up, boils up, effervesces, Cels. 5, 27, 4 : “frena spumantia,” covered with foam, Verg. A. 4, 135 ; 5, 817: “mella,” id. G. 4, 140 : “sanguis,” id. A. 9, 456 .—Of an angry person: “spumantibus ardens visceribus,” Juv. 13, 14 . —
II. Act., to cause to foam, to foam forth, cover with foam (very rare). *
A. Lit.: saxa salis niveo spumata liquore, Cic. Poët. Div. 1, 7, 13.—
B. Trop.: “ex ore scelus,” Auct. Her. 4, 55, 68 ; Claud. Rapt. Pros. 1, 282.
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
